'''Koganeyama Shrine''' (黄金山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.<ref>{{Cite web|title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー|url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/|access-date=2023-04-02|website=jinja-gosyuin.com}}</ref>
{{infobox shinto shrine|religious_affiliation=[[Shinto]]|image=Koganeyama-jinja Haiden.jpg|map_type=Japan|coordinates={{coordinates|38|17|52.9|N|141|33|21.6|E}}|location=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|locale=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|deity=- Kanayamahiko-no-Kami - Kanayamahime-no-Kami - Heavenly Myriad Deities - Earthly Myriad Deities|festivals=September 25|festival=September 25|consecration_year=Year 750 (during the Tenpyo-shoho era)|type=Listed Minor Shrine, Former Prefectural Shrine, [[Beppyo Shrine]]|architecture_type=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing|architecture_style=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing}}
It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] .
== Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == According to the shrine's legend, it was founded as a shrine in the second year [[Tenpyō-shōhō|of the Tenpyo Shoho era]] ( [[750]] ). In [[Nara period|the Nara period]], when the {{ill|10=ja|11=ヤマト王権|Yamato Kingship|lt=Yamato Imperial Court|en}} was struggling to raise [[Gold|the gold]] needed to gild [[Tōdai-ji|the Todaiji Temple]] {{ill|10=ja|11=毘盧遮那仏|Vairocana|en}} statue ( {{ill|10=ja|11=東大寺盧舎那仏像|the Great Buddha of Nara}} ) as a national project, in [[Tenpyō|February]] 749, news of the first gold mine in [[Japan]] and the gold itself were brought from [[Mutsu Province]] <ref>『[[続日本紀]]』同年2月丁巳（22日）条。『[[日本紀略]]』は同年正月4日とする。</ref> . The source of the gold was Mount Kinka, and in the following [[Tenpyō-shōhō|year]], [[750]] <ref>天平21年春の産金を賀して同年4月に「天平」から「[[天平感宝]]」へ、更に7月に「天平勝宝」へと[[改元]]されている。</ref>, Oshika no Muraji Miyamaro and others applied to {{ill|10=ja|11=国司|Kokushi (official)|lt=the provincial governor|en}} of the time to build a shrine to worship the gods in charge of gold mining, and enshrined two gods, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, on Mount Koganeyama. It is said that this shrine later became a temple with Benzaiten as its {{ill|10=ja|11=本尊|Honzon|lt=principal image|en}}. In celebration of this first gold mine in Japan, {{Ill|Ōtomo no Yakamochi|en}} composed the following [[Waka (poetry)|tanka]]:{{Quote frame|"May the Emperor's reign prosper, and golden flowers bloom in the land of Michinoku, to the east."<ref>『[[万葉集]]』巻第18所収、「陸奥国に金を出す[[詔書]]を賀（ほ）く歌一首」(「[[海行かば]]」の原歌でもある)に添えられた「[[反歌]]三首」中の1首（[[国歌大観番号]]4097）。</ref>}}It is said that the name of the island (mountain) was derived from the "golden flower" that can be seen in the sky. Regarding Benzaiten, it is said that she was a celestial maiden who washed ashore on the Pacific coast of Mount Kinka and was enshrined at the top and base of the mountain, with the base called Benzaiten-do (Daikoku-ji Temple) and the top called Ryuzo Gongen (now Owatatsumi Shrine) <ref>宮田「金華山信仰とミロク」（『ミロク信仰の研究』第1章第5節）。天女の漂着地はいずれも金華山島東部海岸に位置する御船沢とも、銀波越または金波越とも、大函（箱）崎ともいう。</ref> . There is also a legend that King Keibok of Baekje, who presented the gold he produced to the {{ill|10=ja|11=百済王敬福|Imperial Court}}, washed ashore at Omaehama Beach in [[Onagawa, Miyagi|the town of Onagawa]], near the northern base of the Oshika Peninsula <ref name="宮田">宮田前掲論文。</ref>, or that he lived in the same place <ref name="大槻">[[大槻茂質]]『夢遊金華山之記』、文化9年（1812年）。</ref> .
Until the Edo period, the origins of this shrine (then a temple) were widely accepted, and the Koganeyama Shrine in Oda District of Mutsu Province, a listed shrine, was thought to have been established based on the gold mining there, which led to its identification as "Koganeyama Shrine." However, in 1813 (the 10th year of the Bunka era), Okin Yasumi, a Kokugaku scholar from Ise Province, determined that the original site of the Tenpyo-era gold production was in the current Wakuya Town of Ota District, Miyagi Prefecture (formerly part of Oda District), where the small Kogane Shrine was located and which he then revived as the historical Koganeyama Shrine. This led to the need to reconsider the origins of the shrine's founding. As a result, the imposing appearance of the mountain, standing in the sea and revered as a spiritual dwelling by the people along the coast of the Oshika Peninsula, was considered a subject of natural worship. The rugged terrain of Mount Kinka, known for its steep five peaks and called "68 Peaks and 48 Valleys," led to the belief that the mountain was a site for esoteric [[Shugendō|Shugendo]] practitioners, particularly from the Heian period onward, many of whom were affiliated with Daikin-ji Temple, founded by Kobo Daishi (Kukai), the founder of the Shingon sect. This area, along with the entire Sanriku Coast, housed many Shingon temples dedicated to Benzaiten, which suggests that these Shugendo practitioners played a significant role in developing the site as a sacred place. They established Daikin-ji Temple, which likely spurred the mountain's development. These practitioners, based on the island's location as the easternmost point of Honshu, envisioned Mount Kinka as a mythical land akin to Mount Penglai or the eternal realm of Tokoyo, a utopia sought after in ancient China and Japan, centering around Daikin-ji Temple and dedicating it to Benzaiten, which linked her divine blessings to the historical facts of Tenpyo-era gold production and the "golden flowers bloom" poem. Additionally, according to the Sendai domain's commissioned geographic record, "Fuchinai Fudoki," originally, Miwa Myojin had built Kinkazan Island by molding gold and setting it with four stakes, enshrining the "true soul" of Amaterasu as "Tomonomi-hime-no-kami," later known as Benzaiten. This account, labeled as an "old theory," was dismissed by the author (Tanabe Nozomu) as a fabrication based on the "upper" volume of the "Kojiki" (Ancient Chronicles of the Kami), considered nonsense by monks and ascetic practitioners. Despite the rejection of the theory that the shrine was a historical Koganeyama Shrine, other theories suggest it might instead be associated with the Oshima Shrine or the Keisenma Shrine in Mutsu Province's Oshika District.
According to the shrine's traditions, around the time of [[Eiman|the Eiman]] to [[Nin'an]] era (mid-12th century), Fujiwara no Hidehira built 48 temples (halls and pagodas) including Daikin-ji Temple and donated 1,000 koku of {{ill|10=ja|11=寺社領|Jisha-ryō|lt=temple land|en}}, making it {{ill|10=ja|11=一山寺院|a mountain temple}} (an independent temple organization consisting of a core temple and multiple shrines and temples) with Daikin-ji Temple at its center <ref>月光善弘「金華山の修験道」（『東北霊山と修験道』所収）。但し神社由緒では秀衡寄進の寺領は3,000石とされる。</ref> . After the fall of the Fujiwara clan, the number of temples and pagodas was reduced to 18 and the temple land to 500 koku by Kasai Kiyoshige, who was appointed as the general magistrate of Oshu and lord of Ishinomaki Castle <ref>神社所蔵大般若経納箱蓋裏墨書（[[黄金山神社 (石巻市)#信仰|#信仰]]参照）。神社由緒は清重安堵の寺領を1,500石とするが、これは蓋裏に記された500石と見るのが妥当と思われる（月光前掲論文）。なお、清重時代の18坊とは、大金寺・大蔵寺・大徳寺・大願寺・大応寺・弁蔵寺・弁教寺・弁明寺・弁寿院・斎蔵坊・斎覚坊・斎性坊・斎沢坊・斎念坊・天竜菴・天聖菴・天経菴・天瑞菴（『封内風土記』）。</ref>, but the temple flourished under his protection. The background to this is thought to be that, in response to the Imperial Court’s development and strategy for [[Tōhoku region|the Tohoku region]] (the so-called Emishi subjugation ) from the Nara period onwards, the ascetic monks who participated as military forces or military monks in the Former Nine Years ’ and Later Three Years’ Wars and who continued to stay in the area thereafter and gathered at Koganeyama as a base for religious activities such as mountain ascetic practices and incantations, were viewed as being able to provide both prayer activities for peace in their territories in peacetime and military forces in wartime, and were therefore protected by local powerful clans, particularly the Fujiwara clan, who claimed dominance over [[Kamakura period|the Tohoku region in late ancient times. The relationship with the feudal lords is thought to have been similar from the Kamakura period]] onwards <ref name="小野寺" /> <ref name="月光">月光前掲論文。</ref> but the state of the temple throughout the Middle Ages is unclear as the old records were lost in several fires. The temple fell into decline due to the wars of [[Sengoku period|the Sengoku period]], and in [[Tenshō (Momoyama period)|the Tensho era]] (late 16th century) all of the temple buildings were burned down in a fire, and in [[Bunroku|1522]] ( It was restored in [[1593]] by the Shugendo monk Choshun Seizobo, who was from Iwakura in [[Shimotsuke Province]] and was also the head priest of Nikko-san ( Rinno-ji Temple ) <ref>『牡鹿郡誌』牡鹿郡役所、大正12年。なお、『封内風土記』は再興を天正年間の事とするが、天正の後が文禄なので時代的には大差がなく、天正元年（1573年）から文禄2年（1593年）の21年間に再興なったものと見られる（月光前掲論文）。</ref> .
During the Edo period, it is said that the island was set aside as a sanctuary and the temple buildings were rebuilt in response to the reverence of the Date clan, feudal lords of the Sendai domain. Under the honmatsu system, it was positioned as a Shugendo temple of the Tozan sect, with Daigo Sanboin as its head temple ( the main temple is Ryuhoji Temple under Sendai Castle). Regarding the reverence shown by the Date clan, there is a record of the fourth feudal lord, Tsunamura, sending his retainers to visit the temple on his behalf for three consecutive months in [[1703]] ( [[Genroku]] 16) to donate gold dust <ref>『[[伊達治家記録|肯山公（綱村）治家記録]]』。</ref>, but perhaps due to geographical conditions such as the distance from the castle town, there was no sign of regular, direct support from the feudal lord. In the end, only Daikin-ji temple remained out of the 18 temples that once numbered <ref>『封内風土記』。</ref>, and as it was a branch temple of Sanboin, its organization and influence as a single mountain temple had been dissolved. As a result, Daikinji Temple, which was trying to maintain its temples and pagodas, needed to actively reach out to the common people. Specifically, it is thought that the temple traveled around villages to promote the blessings of Benzaiten. As a result, faith in Daikinji Temple (Mount Kinka) flourished, and from the mid-Edo period onwards, religious associations were formed in various places and the number of pilgrims increased. <ref name="小野寺" /> However, in 1813, a fire once again reduced the entire mountain to ashes, and the temple buildings were rebuilt to their original appearance with the assistance of the Date clan <ref name="奥海">奥海登和子「金華山信仰」（岩崎敏夫編『東北民俗資料集（四）』所収、萬葉堂書店、昭和50年）。</ref>, but all of the old records were lost during this process.
Following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]], and in response to the Order to Separate Shinto and [[1869|Buddhism,]] Daikin-ji Temple was abolished in [[Meiji period|1869]] and became Koganeyama Shrine, which enshrines the two deities Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime. The head priest of Daikin-ji Temple returned to secular life and became a Shinto priest taking the surname Okumi. In June of the same year, the shrine was ranked as a prefectural shrine. When Daikin-ji Temple was abandoned, all of its Buddhist scriptures and statues were taken off the island. <ref>小野寺前掲論文。金華山対岸山鳥の奥海家に祀られている弁財天の木像はかつての本尊であったと伝えるが、これは文化期の火災後に新たに彫られたものと思われる（小野寺同論文）。なお、文化以前の本尊は元禄11年（1698年）の記録（『牡鹿郡万御改書』）によれば高さ3[[尺]]7[[寸]]（110[[センチメートル|センチ]]強）の木像であった。</ref> The shrine building had been renovated since [[1877]], but in February 1907, a fire broke out in a house near the shrine office, burning down the shrine for the third time, including the trees within the grounds, leaving only [[Shintai|the sacred object]] and [[mikoshi]] ( portable shrine). As a result, starting with the completion of the worship hall in 1916 [[Taishō period|,]] the current shrine building was gradually rebuilt. After the war [[1952|,]] it joined the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]] and became a [[Beppyo shrine]] shrine in [[Shōwa period|1952]] .
== faith == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] Koganeyama was an object of worship for the people living along the coast of the Oshika Peninsula in ancient times, and is thought to have been worshipped especially by fishermen as the guardian deity of fishing and safety at sea. Although this is an example from later times, fishermen engaged in deep sea fishing such as [[Skipjack tuna|bonito]] fishing would call the area where about one third of Koganeyama sank below the horizon (about 20 nautical miles ) "San no gote (Third Palace)," which was then renamed "Nino gote (Second Palace)," and the point where the island's silhouette was small and looked like a star (about 45 nautical miles) was called "Nioboshi (Nyuho star)," and when it was completely below the horizon it was called "Yamanashi (no mountain)." They used Koganeyama as a guide for measuring the distance to fishing grounds, and even when the mountain was in "Yamanashi" where the shape of the mountain could not be seen, it was customary to face Koganeyama at sunset and offer [[Eternal flame|a lamp]] to pray. It is also said that they felt an indescribable sense of relief when they saw "Nioboshi" on their return from the deep seas. <ref name="宮田" /> In addition, before setting out to fish, it is said that prayers are offered at Mount Kinka, and that on island beaches where the mountain's shape can be seen, prayers are always offered at New Year's and other times <ref name="小野寺" /> Also, it is said that ships passing offshore would light lamps, scatter [[rice]] into the sea, and offer prayers, and that when fishing for pacific saury, seven pacific saury would be offered into the sea to pray for safe fishing and a good catch. <ref>『宮城県百科事典』（河北新報社、昭和57年）「金華山信仰」。</ref> Sailors on sea routes also worshipped him as a god for safe voyages. On the voyage of the Kaisei Maru, a warship of the [[Ansei|Sendai]] domain in [[1858]], the sailors chanted "Oyama Oyama" for Mount Kinka, and when they came into view of Daikinji Temple, they washed their hands, rinsed their mouths, and scattered rice into the sea before bowing. <ref>[[小野寺鳳谷]]『開成丸航海日誌』。</ref>
On the other hand, from ancient to medieval times, ascetics gathered at Mount Kinka built Daikin Temple and based themselves there, engaging in rigorous ascetic practices among the peaks. There are no historical records detailing the actual practices of asceticism at Mount Kinka, but it is said that there were places called {{ill|Diamond Realm|ja|金剛界|en}} and "Womb Realm" on the east side of the island, and place names such as "Utero Diving" and "{{ill|Soji Pass|ja|蘇字峠}}" and "Tengu Sumo Wrestling Area" on the island suggest their connection to ascetic practices. The presence of a fire altar beside the Daikaiji Shrine (formerly Ryuzo Gongen) at the summit suggests that such ascetic practices were indeed performed. Particularly, the "Utero Diving" ritual, which sees the mountain as a mother's womb in the philosophy of Shugendo, involved passing through a hole just large enough to crawl through at the base of a large rock, symbolizing a ritual of simulated death and rebirth, thought to confer new spiritual powers<ref name="小野寺" />. Moreover, the "Sai no Kawara" located on the northeast coast of Mount Kinka is said to be a place where one can hear the voices of deceased relatives when visited, similar to the faith in ancestral and spirit spirits held at Yamadera (Risshakuji) in Yamagata Prefecture and Bodaiji in Osorezan, Aomori Prefecture. The faith in Benzaiten at Daikin Temple dates back to an early time, as indicated by the initial letters of the 48 temple names built by Hidehira forming an acrostic for "Daiben Saiten" (Great Benzaiten), recorded in "Fuchinai Fudoki" <ref>However, the actual number of temples listed in the same book is 44, consisting of 19 temples, 4 monasteries, 12 temples, and 9 hermitages (underlined temples persisted during the Kiyoshige era). </ref>. The tradition of Benzaiten, especially along the coastal areas of the Sanriku coast, is commonly associated with drift legends involving river gods (water gods), as mentioned above, suggesting that the original faith in Benzaiten as a water god formed the basis. This is evident in the ancient {{ill|Yorigami faith|ja|寄神信仰}}, primarily held by coastal fishermen who revered drift items from beyond the seas. Such foundational beliefs were overlaid by ascetics with the image of an ideal paradise above the eastern seas, actively promoted to manifest this paradise in reality, emphasizing the wealth-bringing aspect of Benzaiten as a fortune deity, and tying this with the historical fact of Tenpyo gold production and the prosperity brought by the "golden flowers bloom" song<ref name="宮田" />. {{Quote box|### Relics Part 1: '''Soji Pass''' [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] Soji Pass is located in the eastern mountains of Mount Kinka. It was a sacred place inaccessible to laypeople, where the founding monk (Narizo-bo Chojun) performed the "Thousand-Day Circumambulation." At its base, there exists an ideology of a utopia deep within the mountains, akin to a hidden village view, suggesting a kind of secluded paradise. However, this might have been further localized and minimized into a "quintessentially early-modern production" after the image of Mount Kinka as a golden and silver island was formed during the Edo period. <ref name="宮田"/>。|width=30%}}The result of these efforts was the expansion of the area of faith in Mount Kinka in the early modern period, but on the inside of the lid of the Great Hannya Sutra storage box dated [[1583]] and still kept at Kinkazan Shrine, there is an inscribed mandala featuring [[Mandala|Benzaiten]], who was widely known in the Middle Ages, surrounded by other deities of good fortune, proving that the connection between Daikinji Temple and the people through the faith in Benzaiten as a deity of good fortune also dates back to before the early modern period <ref name="宮田" /> .
'''Belief in Mount Kinka''' became popular in the early modern period. The background to this is thought to be that Daikinji Temple and the ascetic monks based there, feeling a sense of crisis after losing the active protection from powerful people such as feudal lords and feudal lords, sought to expand the area of their faith by appealing to the general public in order to maintain the temple's management <ref name="小野寺" /> <ref name="月光" /> Alternatively, the people who accepted the faith also had a longing for a savior unique to Japan who would bring about a better world, specifically <u>Miroku</u>, who brings abundant crops and appears in the verses of the Kashima Odori dance distributed along the coasts of the [[Kantō region|Kanto]] and Tokai regions There was a belief that Miroku would appear in the year of [[Snake (zodiac)|the snake]] or on the day of the snake, and a custom of forming groups such as "Mi- machi- ko" (a meeting place for snakes) on the day of the snake or the day before it to await the arrival of Miroku. In contrast, Daikonji Benzaiten was also considered to [[Shinshi|have a]] divine role as a water deity, and so a large-scale ritual was held in the year of the snake, in which [[Snake|a snake]] -year festival was held. Therefore, it is thought that as ascetics, utilizing the associations of "Miroku," "snake," "snake," and "Benzaiten," assimilated Benzaiten faith into village faith and expanded the sphere of faith by transforming the existing Mi-machi-ko into '''Koganeyama-ko''' <ref name="宮田" /> . In addition, it seems that Daikin-ji Temple sometimes held public exhibitions of statues of Benzaiten to raise funds for its temples, and there are temples where the Benzaiten statues were then made into principal images at the exhibition locations. <ref>小野寺前掲論文。例せば石巻市の[[寿福寺 (石巻市)|寿福寺]]に祀られる弁財天像は[[厨子]]内に安置されているが、元は大金寺からの出開帳の際の尊像で、金華山からの遠路の労を省いて当寺に安置されるようになったもので、持ち運びの便を図って厨子に納められていた為に厨子ごと祀られるようになったという。</ref>
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|### Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== From the mid-early modern period onwards, pilgrims seeking the blessings of Benzaiten came not only from within Sendai Domain but also from other provinces. The pilgrimage route from Sendai to Ishinomaki and then to Mount Kinka was recorded in contemporary travel guidebooks such as "Various Directions and Routes" and "Travel Records of Various Provinces." According to these records, the journey to Ishinomaki largely utilized the Ishinomaki Road, from where it split into land and sea routes. It is speculated that the subsequent routes included the Omotehama Road, which went along the western coast of the Oshika Peninsula either by land or sea to Ayukawa at the southwestern tip, and the Urahama Road, which went by land down the eastern coast of the peninsula to Yamadori. Although it was possible to go directly by sea to Mount Kinka on both routes, it was customary to take the land route as a test of faith. Even when taking the sea route on the Omotehama Road, pilgrims would disembark at Ayukawa and then cross the Komagamine Pass to reach Yamadori, passing through the first torii gate there before crossing the strait (also known as the Yamadori Strait or Kinka Strait) to the island, where, if a bell was rung upon gathering at Yamadori, a boat would come from the island to fetch them. However, the area around Mount Kinka was known for its strong tidal currents and treacherous waters, and many shipwrecks had occurred historically; on stormy nights, it was said that the ghosts of the drowned would approach ships in operation and ask for a ladle. Even though the Yamadori crossing was short, large waves called "Palace Hiding" often made it too rough, and if the seas were too violent, no boats could come from Mount Kinka, forcing pilgrims to return to Ayukawa to wait. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims were required to change into new straw sandals before disembarking to avoid bringing worldly impurities onto the sacred island, then they would visit Daikin Temple<ref name="奥海" />, and if they were to proceed to the island’s climbing pilgrimage sites (described later), they would stay overnight at Daikin Temple and depart for the climbing the next morning<ref name="小野寺" />. Mount Kinka was believed to be made of gold, and when departing the island after completing their pilgrimage, it was taboo to take anything off the island—from gold and other minerals to even a single blade of grass or a grain of sand, as "the island god cherishes them."<ref name="奥海" /> Pilgrims would leave their straw sandals on the pier<ref name="奥海" />, and it was said that if they disobeyed, their return boat would either not move or sink<ref name="小野寺" />. Although unverified, there is an anecdote about Kiuchi Sekitei who, after visiting Mount Kinka and secretly pocketing some gold sand, found that the boat he boarded could not progress through rough waves. When the boatman investigated and discovered the theft, Sekitei had no choice but to return the gold sand<ref>Suzuki Tōzai, Tachibana, "Eastern Travel Journal," Supplemental Notes (Volume 20 of the Japanese Folk Life Material Collection, San'ichi Shobo, 1972). Afterwards, Sekitei prayed to the island god for permission to take the sand for academic purposes, and he was able to bring it back successfully.</ref>. The custom of leaving sandals reflects the strong notion of sanctity associated with Mount Kinka. Even when a monk from Daikin Temple passed away, he was never buried on the island; instead, his remains were transported across to Yamadori. Furthermore, women were strictly forbidden from crossing to the island, and they would worship the mountain from the first torii gate at Yamadori.
Furthermore, groups called Koganeyama ko were formed in various places for the purpose of worshiping Koganeyama, but some appear to have been transformed from existing ko organizations, and some of them were called Mimachi ko, and involved various religious activities centered around the day of the snake. As membership in the group was restricted to men, due to the idea that women were not allowed to join, the group was mainly made up of heads of households, and on the opening days, which were held several times a year, members would gather at designated lodgings on a rotation basis, where they would hang a hanging scroll of Mt. Kinka on the upper seat, such as the tokonoma alcove in the tatami room, use it as an altar, light a lamp, offer [[Omiki|sacred sake]], pray amongst the group, and then dine on vegetarian cuisine . In remote villages where it is difficult to make the pilgrimage to Mt. Kinka for financial or other reasons, a proxy is chosen to represent the group (usually two people), and the proxy who makes the pilgrimage distributes the sacred talismans that are given to the group members. As pilgrimages to Mt. Kinka were made repeatedly, stone monuments commemorating them would be erected at village entrances, crossroads, or within the grounds of local shrines, and Benzaiten would sometimes be enshrined in [[Hokora|small shrines]] within the grounds of local shrines or as the deity of the household . There are various types of Kinkazan ko in various regions, with some continuing from the time of their formation and others disbanding after a certain period of time, but in modern times there are about 500 ko of various sizes in the Tohoku prefectures, mainly Miyagi, as well as in [[Hokkaidō|Hokkaido]] and [[Chiba Prefecture|Chiba prefectures]] . In [[1921]], Kinkazan Shrine reorganized existing ko to form the "Eitaiko" organization with the aim of reviving the shrine and expanding its sphere of faith. <ref name="小野寺" />
Furthermore, the idea that gold could not have been produced from Mt. Kinka, and the historical fact of gold mining in the Tenpyo period was denied in the mid-Edo period. However, there were still many people who held the illusion of an island made of gold up until the end of the Taisho period, as sung in the Toshima Jinku (a chant from a distant island) that was often sung in the Oshika district during the Meiji and Taisho periods, such as "On Mt. Kinka, there are big boxes and small boxes of gold, and then there is gold as well," and "When a wind of a good catch blows offshore, golden flowers bloom on the island." Similarly, in Matsusakabushi (also known as Matsushimabushi), there was a song that sang, "Mt. Kinka to the east is a mountain of gold." <ref name="宮田" />
== Rituals == The annual festival is held on September 25th, but there are also other Shinto rituals and festivals such as the following:
; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to [[潮垢離|purify the shrine]] . This is also a type of [[浜降神事|Hamadori ritual]], and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
== Shrine == The main hall is in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall is a gabled roof style with five bays across and three beams, and a three-bay veranda with a gabled roof in the center at the front. Both have copper roofs. Other buildings include a prayer hall and a Suishinmon gate, and in the prayer hall, goma wood is burned and prayers are offered by petitioners, just as in the Shugendo period.
The current shrine buildings were rebuilt piecemeal over a period of 30 years following a fire in 1897. Incidentally, the shrine buildings before the fire (the ones newly rebuilt in the 1870s) were extremely beautiful in terms of their architecture and sculptures, and were even called the “ [[Shrines and Temples of Nikkō|Nikko]] of the Eastern Frontier” <ref>『角川日本地名大辞典4 宮城県』角川書店、昭和54年。</ref> . The site of Daikin-ji Temple is located to the west of the main hall. <ref name="宮田" />
The pair of bronze lanterns standing in front of the worship hall are one each donated in 1892 and 1894 by worshippers living in [[Yamagata|Yamagata City, Yamagata]] Prefecture, and both were cast in Domachi, Yamagata City. It is 4.8 [[Metre|meters]] tall and is known as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," along with those at [[Kotohira-gū|Kotohira Shrine]] ( [[Kagawa Prefecture]] ) and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple (Yamagata Prefecture) <ref>[http://www5.ocn.ne.jp/~kinkasan/jouyatou.html 金華山黄金山神社「常夜燈」]（平成23年5月30日閲覧）。</ref> .
== Temple grounds == The entire island of Mount Kinka was considered a sacred area, and in the early modern period, Ryuzo Gongen was enshrined at the summit of Mount Kinka as the inner sanctum, with Benzaiten at the center. Other universal deities and Buddhas such as Atago Gongen, [[Shinmei shrines|Shinmeigu Shrine]], and Fudo Hall were enshrined in various places on the island, and Mount Kinka itself was considered a sacred island, with Daikinji Temple as its chief priest and governing it. <ref>前掲『宮城県百科事典』「金華山」。</ref> In addition, the entire island of Mount Kinka, including the temple grounds, was designated a quasi-national park in [[1979]] (part of Minamisanriku Kinkazan Quasi-National Park ), and in [[2015]] it was designated a national park following its incorporation into Sanriku Fukko National Park .
=== Main shrines within the precincts ===
; {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|大海祇神社}} : Located at the summit of Mount Kinka as the inner sanctuary. Formerly known as Ryuuzo Sansha Daigongen Shrine, it worshipped the guardian deity of the sea, believed to be an incarnation of the Eleven-Faced Kannon, and, according to other legends, either Benzaiten or Zao Gongen were also enshrined. After the Meiji period, the shrine was reorganized to enshrine four deities: {{ill|Watatsumi|ja|大綿津見神}}, {{ill|Ichikishimahime|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ichikishimahime|fr}} (who was regarded as an incarnation of Benzaiten during the syncretic period of Shinto and Buddhism), Heaven's Pillar God: Ame no Mimashira no Kami (天之御柱神) and Country's Pillar God: Kuni no Mimashira no Kami (国之御柱神). The main hall is built in the Shinto architectural style with a copper roof, measuring one ken in width and two ken in depth, and features a slightly narrower worship hall extending from the front. The annual festival takes place on March 18th. : Near the shrine, a fire altar facing the eastern sea, showing remnants of Shugendo rituals, is set up where fire rituals continue to be performed at sunrise.
; {{ill|Kanagui Shrine|ja|樁神社}} : Located in a cedar grove on the south side of the stone steps leading from the gate to the worship hall. It is a shrine originating from the creation myths recorded in "Fuchinai Fudoki" and is considered the guardian shrine of Koganeyama Shrine. After the Meiji period, it began enshrining twelve deities, including {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴神}}. The main hall, the most intricately constructed among the subsidiary shrines, is a square building with a copper roof. The annual festival is held on June 25th.
; {{ill|Hama Shrine|ja|濱神社}} : Located on the western slope of the sanctuary, this shrine enshrines {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|言代主神}} (also known as {{ill|Ebisu|ja|恵比須尊}}). In the past, it was situated on the Turtle Rock in Kinkazan Port and was worshipped by fishermen who hoped for a good catch at the start of the fishing season, regularly offering fishes and other items. The current Turtle Rock has become connected to the mainland by a dyke, but previously, access required a small boat. It seems that the shrine was moved inland due to the difficulties of visiting it in modern times. The main hall is a square building with a flat copper roof. The annual festival is on July 10th. Additionally, Turtle Rock, also historically known as Turtle Island, is associated with a legend: during the period when women were forbidden on the Oshika Peninsula, a woman named Kame attempted to cross to the island, swimming over from Yamadori. As she tried to land, she was turned into stone by the wrath of the gods<ref name="月光" />.
Prayers also take part in "mountain climbing" tours, which can be broadly divided into two categories, the front walk and the back walk. The front walk starts from the sub-shrine Nameraishi Shrine behind the main hall, goes around the strangely shaped rocks and stones in the mountains, and reaches Shobudaira, then climbs to the top of Musou Peak to pay homage to Daimigami Shrine. The back path starts from Musomine, similarly paying homage to the giant rocks, passes through Tainai-shi, passes unusual rocks such as Kaisan Shonin Zazen-seki and Yamagata-seki, and then descends to the east coast, going around Senjojiki, Sennin-zawa, Ohakozaki, and Sainokawara along the eastern coast, before crossing Amida Pass and returning to the main hall <ref>『神道大辞典』第2巻（平凡社、昭和14年）「黄金山神社」。</ref> .
As of [[2007]], there are approximately 530 wild deer living on the island, and they are protected as messengers of the gods. However, there is a legend that [[Date Masamune]], the first lord of the Sendai domain, hunted deer on Mount Kinka <ref>前掲『東北民俗資料集（四）』。</ref>, which would mean that hunting was carried out in ancient times and the animals were not protected. However, in the late Edo period, there is a legend that 1,000 beaters were drowned in the sea as divine punishment for deer hunting <ref name="大槻" />, so it is thought that they came to be regarded as messengers of the gods in early modern times and later. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu01.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref> In addition, the deity enshrined at the Nameshi Shrine within the precincts ( Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ) is [[:ja:分霊|a branch deity]] of [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima-jingu Shrine]] [[Ibaraki Prefecture|in Ibaraki Prefecture]], and since the shrine has a close relationship with deer, it has been speculated that the deer of Mount Kinka were also viewed as divine messengers. <ref>『牡鹿町誌』下巻、牡鹿町、平成14年。</ref>
