<ref name="小野寺" /><ref name="小野寺">小野寺正人「金華山信仰の展開」（『東北霊山と修験道』所収）。</ref>
'''Koganeyama Shrine''' (黄金山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.<ref>{{Cite web|title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー|url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/|access-date=2023-04-02|website=jinja-gosyuin.com}}</ref>
{{infobox shinto shrine|religious_affiliation=[[Shinto]]|image=Koganeyama-jinja Haiden.jpg|map_type=Japan|coordinates={{coordinates|38|17|52.9|N|141|33|21.6|E}}|location=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|locale=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|deity=- Kanayamahiko-no-Kami - Kanayamahime-no-Kami - Heavenly Myriad Deities - Earthly Myriad Deities|festivals=September 25|festival=September 25|consecration_year=Year 750 (during the Tenpyo-shoho era)|type=Listed Minor Shrine, Former Prefectural Shrine, [[Beppyo Shrine]]|architecture_type=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing|architecture_style=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing}}
It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] . == Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == Koganeyama Shrine was established in the second year of the Tenpyo Shoho era (750 AD) near the site of Japan's first gold mine on Mount Kinka, vital for funding national projects like the gilding of the Todaiji Temple's Great Buddha. Initially, the shrine was dedicated to the gods of gold mining, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, and later became associated with Benzaiten, embodying prosperity and good fortune.
Legend ties the shrine to celestial origins, suggesting Benzaiten was a celestial maiden who inspired the shrine's location. Over centuries, the shrine's influence grew, supported by the Fujiwara clan among others, and became a center for Shugendo practitioners, linking spiritual practices with the region's rich gold deposits.
Despite various reconstructions due to fire and war, the shrine's cultural and spiritual significance persisted. Following the Meiji Restoration, it transitioned from a Buddhist temple to a Shinto shrine, reflecting broader religious reforms of the period. The shrine buildings, repeatedly damaged and rebuilt, today continue to serve as a site of pilgrimage and cultural heritage, closely tied to the community and the natural landscape of the region.
== Religious practices == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] Historically, Koganeyama has been a central figure in the religious life of people along the Oshika Peninsula, particularly among fishermen who revered it as a guardian deity for safety and prosperity at sea. Sailors used the mountain as a navigational guide, naming different points of its visibility at sea to estimate their distance from the coast. Rituals such as lighting lamps at sunset and offering prayers and rice into the sea were common, underscoring the mountain's deep spiritual significance.
Ascetic practices were also prevalent at Mount Kinka, where ascetics engaged in rigorous spiritual exercises. Locations like the "Diamond Realm" and "Womb Realm" on the island suggest a strong tradition of esoteric Buddhism, with rituals like the "Utero Diving" symbolizing death and rebirth. This spiritual tradition, centered around the temple at Mount Kinka, attracted pilgrims and fostered a community that believed deeply in the sacred powers of the mountain and its deities, particularly Benzaiten. Over time, these practices evolved, blending with local legends and the mythology of Benzaiten as a deity of water and wealth, further enriching the cultural tapestry of the region.
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== Pilgrims from Sendai Domain and beyond have traveled to Koganeyama Shrine for centuries, following established routes documented in travel guides like "Various Directions and Routes." The journey from Sendai to Ishinomaki splits into land and sea paths at Ishinomaki, leading to Ayukawa and then to Mount Kinka via the Omotehama and Urahama Roads. Traditional practices require land travel as a test of faith, although sea routes are also used. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims change into new straw sandals to purify themselves before visiting Daikin Temple. Strict traditions prevent removing any natural elements from the island, reflecting its sacred status. Additionally, local groups known as Koganeyama ko conduct regular worship and community gatherings, reinforcing the shrine's cultural importance. Legends and songs imbue the island with mythical qualities, celebrating its historical association with gold and prosperity.
== Rituals == The annual festival is held on September 25th, but there are also other Shinto rituals and festivals such as the following:
; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to purify the shrine . This is also a type of Hamadori ritual, and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
== Shrine == The main hall is in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall is a gabled roof style with five bays across and three beams, and a three-bay veranda with a gabled roof in the center at the front. Both have copper roofs. Other buildings include a prayer hall and a Suishinmon gate, and in the prayer hall, goma wood is burned and prayers are offered by petitioners, just as in the Shugendo period.
The current shrine buildings were rebuilt piecemeal over a period of 30 years following a fire in 1897. Incidentally, the shrine buildings before the fire (the ones newly rebuilt in the 1870s) were extremely beautiful in terms of their architecture and sculptures, and were even called the “ [[Shrines and Temples of Nikkō|Nikko]] of the Eastern Frontier” <ref>『角川日本地名大辞典4 宮城県』角川書店、昭和54年。</ref> . The site of Daikin-ji Temple is located to the west of the main hall. <ref name="宮田" />
The pair of bronze lanterns standing in front of the worship hall are one each donated in 1892 and 1894 by worshippers living in [[Yamagata|Yamagata City, Yamagata]] Prefecture, and both were cast in Domachi, Yamagata City. It is 4.8 [[Metre|meters]] tall and is known as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," along with those at [[Kotohira-gū|Kotohira Shrine]] ( [[Kagawa Prefecture]] ) and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple (Yamagata Prefecture) <ref>[http://www5.ocn.ne.jp/~kinkasan/jouyatou.html 金華山黄金山神社「常夜燈」]（平成23年5月30日閲覧）。</ref> .
== Temple grounds == The entire island of Mount Kinka was considered a sacred area, and in the early modern period, Ryuzo Gongen was enshrined at the summit of Mount Kinka as the inner sanctum, with Benzaiten at the center. Other universal deities and Buddhas such as Atago Gongen, [[Shinmei shrines|Shinmeigu Shrine]], and Fudo Hall were enshrined in various places on the island, and Mount Kinka itself was considered a sacred island, with Daikinji Temple as its chief priest and governing it. <ref>前掲『宮城県百科事典』「金華山」。</ref> In addition, the entire island of Mount Kinka, including the temple grounds, was designated a quasi-national park in [[1979]] (part of Minamisanriku Kinkazan Quasi-National Park ), and in [[2015]] it was designated a national park following its incorporation into Sanriku Fukko National Park .
=== Main shrines within the precincts ===
; {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine|ja|大海祇神社}} : Located at the summit of Mount Kinka as the inner sanctuary. Formerly known as Ryuuzo Sansha Daigongen Shrine, it worshipped the guardian deity of the sea, believed to be an incarnation of the Eleven-Faced Kannon, and, according to other legends, either Benzaiten or Zao Gongen were also enshrined. After the Meiji period, the shrine was reorganized to enshrine four deities: {{ill|Watatsumi|ja|大綿津見神}}, {{ill|Ichikishimahime|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ichikishimahime|fr}} (who was regarded as an incarnation of Benzaiten during the syncretic period of Shinto and Buddhism), Heaven's Pillar God: Ame no Mimashira no Kami (天之御柱神) and Country's Pillar God: Kuni no Mimashira no Kami (国之御柱神). The main hall is built in the Shinto architectural style with a copper roof, measuring one ken in width and two ken in depth, and features a slightly narrower worship hall extending from the front. The annual festival takes place on March 18th. : Near the shrine, a fire altar facing the eastern sea, showing remnants of Shugendo rituals, is set up where fire rituals continue to be performed at sunrise.
; {{ill|Kanagui Shrine|ja|樁神社}} : Located in a cedar grove on the south side of the stone steps leading from the gate to the worship hall. It is a shrine originating from the creation myths recorded in "Fuchinai Fudoki" and is considered the guardian shrine of Koganeyama Shrine. After the Meiji period, it began enshrining twelve deities, including {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴神}}. The main hall, the most intricately constructed among the subsidiary shrines, is a square building with a copper roof. The annual festival is held on June 25th.
; {{ill|Hama Shrine|ja|濱神社}} : Located on the western slope of the sanctuary, this shrine enshrines {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|言代主神}} (also known as {{ill|Ebisu|ja|恵比須尊}}). In the past, it was situated on the Turtle Rock in Kinkazan Port and was worshipped by fishermen who hoped for a good catch at the start of the fishing season, regularly offering fishes and other items. The current Turtle Rock has become connected to the mainland by a dyke, but previously, access required a small boat. It seems that the shrine was moved inland due to the difficulties of visiting it in modern times. The main hall is a square building with a flat copper roof. The annual festival is on July 10th. Additionally, Turtle Rock, also historically known as Turtle Island, is associated with a legend: during the period when women were forbidden on the Oshika Peninsula, a woman named Kame attempted to cross to the island, swimming over from Yamadori. As she tried to land, she was turned into stone by the wrath of the gods<ref name="月光" />.
Prayers also take part in "mountain climbing" tours, which can be broadly divided into two categories, the front walk and the back walk. The front walk starts from the sub-shrine Nameraishi Shrine behind the main hall, goes around the strangely shaped rocks and stones in the mountains, and reaches Shobudaira, then climbs to the top of Musou Peak to pay homage to Daimigami Shrine. The back path starts from Musomine, similarly paying homage to the giant rocks, passes through Tainai-shi, passes unusual rocks such as Kaisan Shonin Zazen-seki and Yamagata-seki, and then descends to the east coast, going around Senjojiki, Sennin-zawa, Ohakozaki, and Sainokawara along the eastern coast, before crossing Amida Pass and returning to the main hall <ref>『神道大辞典』第2巻（平凡社、昭和14年）「黄金山神社」。</ref> .
As of [[2007]], there are approximately 530 wild deer living on the island, and they are protected as messengers of the gods. However, there is a legend that [[Date Masamune]], the first lord of the Sendai domain, hunted deer on Mount Kinka <ref>前掲『東北民俗資料集（四）』。</ref>, which would mean that hunting was carried out in ancient times and the animals were not protected. However, in the late Edo period, there is a legend that 1,000 beaters were drowned in the sea as divine punishment for deer hunting <ref name="大槻" />, so it is thought that they came to be regarded as messengers of the gods in early modern times and later. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu01.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref> In addition, the deity enshrined at the Nameshi Shrine within the precincts ( Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ) is [[:ja:分霊|a branch deity]] of [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima-jingu Shrine]] [[Ibaraki Prefecture|in Ibaraki Prefecture]], and since the shrine has a close relationship with deer, it has been speculated that the deer of Mount Kinka were also viewed as divine messengers. <ref>『牡鹿町誌』下巻、牡鹿町、平成14年。</ref>

<ref name="小野寺" /><ref name="小野寺">小野寺正人「金華山信仰の展開」（『東北霊山と修験道』所収）。</ref>
'''Koganeyama Shrine''' (黄金山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.<ref>{{Cite web|title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー|url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/|access-date=2023-04-02|website=jinja-gosyuin.com}}</ref>
{{infobox shinto shrine|religious_affiliation=[[Shinto]]|image=Koganeyama-jinja Haiden.jpg|map_type=Japan|coordinates={{coordinates|38|17|52.9|N|141|33|21.6|E}}|location=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|locale=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|deity=- Kanayamahiko-no-Kami - Kanayamahime-no-Kami - Heavenly Myriad Deities - Earthly Myriad Deities|festivals=September 25|festival=September 25|consecration_year=Year 750 (during the Tenpyo-shoho era)|type=Listed Minor Shrine, Former Prefectural Shrine, [[Beppyo Shrine]]|architecture_type=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing|architecture_style=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing}}
It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] . == Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == Koganeyama Shrine was established in the second year of the Tenpyo Shoho era (750 AD) near the site of Japan's first gold mine on Mount Kinka, vital for funding national projects like the gilding of the Todaiji Temple's Great Buddha. Initially, the shrine was dedicated to the gods of gold mining, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, and later became associated with Benzaiten, embodying prosperity and good fortune.
Legend ties the shrine to celestial origins, suggesting Benzaiten was a celestial maiden who inspired the shrine's location. Over centuries, the shrine's influence grew, supported by the Fujiwara clan among others, and became a center for Shugendo practitioners, linking spiritual practices with the region's rich gold deposits.
Despite various reconstructions due to fire and war, the shrine's cultural and spiritual significance persisted. Following the Meiji Restoration, it transitioned from a Buddhist temple to a Shinto shrine, reflecting broader religious reforms of the period. The shrine buildings, repeatedly damaged and rebuilt, today continue to serve as a site of pilgrimage and cultural heritage, closely tied to the community and the natural landscape of the region.
== Religious practices == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] Historically, Koganeyama has been a central figure in the religious life of people along the Oshika Peninsula, particularly among fishermen who revered it as a guardian deity for safety and prosperity at sea. Sailors used the mountain as a navigational guide, naming different points of its visibility at sea to estimate their distance from the coast. Rituals such as lighting lamps at sunset and offering prayers and rice into the sea were common, underscoring the mountain's deep spiritual significance.
Ascetic practices were also prevalent at Mount Kinka, where ascetics engaged in rigorous spiritual exercises. Locations like the "Diamond Realm" and "Womb Realm" on the island suggest a strong tradition of esoteric Buddhism, with rituals like the "Utero Diving" symbolizing death and rebirth. This spiritual tradition, centered around the temple at Mount Kinka, attracted pilgrims and fostered a community that believed deeply in the sacred powers of the mountain and its deities, particularly Benzaiten. Over time, these practices evolved, blending with local legends and the mythology of Benzaiten as a deity of water and wealth, further enriching the cultural tapestry of the region.
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== Pilgrims from Sendai Domain and beyond have traveled to Koganeyama Shrine for centuries, following established routes documented in travel guides like "Various Directions and Routes." The journey from Sendai to Ishinomaki splits into land and sea paths at Ishinomaki, leading to Ayukawa and then to Mount Kinka via the Omotehama and Urahama Roads. Traditional practices require land travel as a test of faith, although sea routes are also used. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims change into new straw sandals to purify themselves before visiting Daikin Temple. Strict traditions prevent removing any natural elements from the island, reflecting its sacred status. Additionally, local groups known as Koganeyama ko conduct regular worship and community gatherings, reinforcing the shrine's cultural importance. Legends and songs imbue the island with mythical qualities, celebrating its historical association with gold and prosperity.
== Rituals == The annual festival is held on September 25th, but there are also other Shinto rituals and festivals such as the following:
; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to purify the shrine . This is also a type of Hamadori ritual, and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
== Shrine == The main hall is in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall is a gabled roof style with five bays across and three beams, and a three-bay veranda with a gabled roof in the center at the front. Both have copper roofs. Other buildings include a prayer hall and a Suishinmon gate, and in the prayer hall, goma wood is burned and prayers are offered by petitioners, just as in the Shugendo period.
The current shrine buildings were rebuilt piecemeal over a period of 30 years following a fire in 1897. Incidentally, the shrine buildings before the fire (the ones newly rebuilt in the 1870s) were extremely beautiful in terms of their architecture and sculptures, and were even called the “ [[Shrines and Temples of Nikkō|Nikko]] of the Eastern Frontier” <ref>『角川日本地名大辞典4 宮城県』角川書店、昭和54年。</ref> . The site of Daikin-ji Temple is located to the west of the main hall. <ref name="宮田" />
The pair of bronze lanterns standing in front of the worship hall are one each donated in 1892 and 1894 by worshippers living in [[Yamagata|Yamagata City, Yamagata]] Prefecture, and both were cast in Domachi, Yamagata City. It is 4.8 [[Metre|meters]] tall and is known as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," along with those at [[Kotohira-gū|Kotohira Shrine]] ( [[Kagawa Prefecture]] ) and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple (Yamagata Prefecture) <ref>[http://www5.ocn.ne.jp/~kinkasan/jouyatou.html 金華山黄金山神社「常夜燈」]（平成23年5月30日閲覧）。</ref> .
== Temple grounds == Mount Kinka and its entire island have long been revered as sacred, with numerous shrines and deities scattered across its landscape, including Ryuzo Gongen at the summit and Benzaiten, the deity of water and wealth, as central figures. The island houses various other deities in shrines like Watatsumi Shrine, Kanagui Shrine, and Hama Shrine, each associated with specific cultural and natural aspects of the region.
Designated a quasi-national park in 1979 and incorporated into Sanriku Fukko National Park in 2015, the area protects its rich religious and natural heritage. Key annual festivals are held in these shrines, continuing traditions that date back centuries. The temple grounds are also a site for unique 'mountain climbing' tours, which explore both the spiritual and physical elements of the landscape.
Protected as messengers of the gods, approximately 530 wild deer live on the island, reflecting the deep spiritual connection between the local wildlife and the shrine's practices. Historical and modern legends surrounding these deer emphasize their sacred status and the area's ongoing cultural significance.

According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== Pilgrims from Sendai Domain and beyond have traveled to Koganeyama Shrine for centuries, following established routes documented in travel guides like "Various Directions and Routes." The journey from Sendai to Ishinomaki splits into land and sea paths at Ishinomaki, leading to Ayukawa and then to Mount Kinka via the Omotehama and Urahama Roads. Traditional practices require land travel as a test of faith, although sea routes are also used. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims change into new straw sandals to purify themselves before visiting Daikin Temple. Strict traditions prevent removing any natural elements from the island, reflecting its sacred status. Additionally, local groups known as Koganeyama ko conduct regular worship and community gatherings, reinforcing the shrine's cultural importance. Legends and songs imbue the island with mythical qualities, celebrating its historical association with gold and prosperity.
== Rituals == The annual festival is held on September 25th, but there are also other Shinto rituals and festivals such as the following:
; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to purify the shrine . This is also a type of Hamadori ritual, and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
==Shrine Architecture and Features== The main hall of the shrine is designed in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall features a gabled roof with five bays across and a three-bay veranda, also with a gabled roof at the front. Both structures are topped with copper roofs. Additional buildings include a prayer hall, where goma wood is burned for prayers in a manner reminiscent of the Shugendo period, and a Suishinmon gate.
The shrine complex was gradually reconstructed over thirty years following a devastating fire in 1897. The architecture prior to this event was highly ornate, comparable in beauty to the renowned Nikko shrines, earning it the nickname "Nikko of the Eastern Frontier." Adjacent to the main hall is the site of the historic Daikin-ji Temple.
Adding to the shrine's historical allure are two bronze lanterns donated by worshippers from Yamagata Prefecture in the late 19th century. Standing 4.8 meters tall, these lanterns are celebrated as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," sharing this distinction with those at Kotohira Shrine and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple.
== Temple grounds == Mount Kinka and its entire island have long been revered as sacred, with numerous shrines and deities scattered across its landscape, including Ryuzo Gongen at the summit and Benzaiten, the deity of water and wealth, as central figures. The island houses various other deities in shrines like Watatsumi Shrine, Kanagui Shrine, and Hama Shrine, each associated with specific cultural and natural aspects of the region.
Designated a quasi-national park in 1979 and incorporated into Sanriku Fukko National Park in 2015, the area protects its rich religious and natural heritage. Key annual festivals are held in these shrines, continuing traditions that date back centuries. The temple grounds are also a site for unique 'mountain climbing' tours, which explore both the spiritual and physical elements of the landscape.
Protected as messengers of the gods, approximately 530 wild deer live on the island, reflecting the deep spiritual connection between the local wildlife and the shrine's practices. Historical and modern legends surrounding these deer emphasize their sacred status and the area's ongoing cultural significance.

'''Koganeyama Shrine''' (黄金山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.<ref>{{Cite web|title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー|url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/|access-date=2023-04-02|website=jinja-gosyuin.com}}</ref>
{{infobox shinto shrine|religious_affiliation=[[Shinto]]|image=Koganeyama-jinja Haiden.jpg|map_type=Japan|coordinates={{coordinates|38|17|52.9|N|141|33|21.6|E}}|location=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|locale=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|deity=- Kanayamahiko-no-Kami - Kanayamahime-no-Kami - Heavenly Myriad Deities - Earthly Myriad Deities|festivals=September 25|festival=September 25|consecration_year=Year 750 (during the Tenpyo-shoho era)|type=Listed Minor Shrine, Former Prefectural Shrine, [[Beppyo Shrine]]|architecture_type=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing|architecture_style=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing}}
It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] . == Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == Koganeyama Shrine was established in the second year of the Tenpyo Shoho era (750 AD) near the site of Japan's first gold mine on Mount Kinka, vital for funding national projects like the gilding of the Todaiji Temple's Great Buddha. Initially, the shrine was dedicated to the gods of gold mining, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, and later became associated with Benzaiten, embodying prosperity and good fortune.
Legend ties the shrine to celestial origins, suggesting Benzaiten was a celestial maiden who inspired the shrine's location. Over centuries, the shrine's influence grew, supported by the Fujiwara clan among others, and became a center for Shugendo practitioners, linking spiritual practices with the region's rich gold deposits.
Despite various reconstructions due to fire and war, the shrine's cultural and spiritual significance persisted. Following the Meiji Restoration, it transitioned from a Buddhist temple to a Shinto shrine, reflecting broader religious reforms of the period. The shrine buildings, repeatedly damaged and rebuilt, today continue to serve as a site of pilgrimage and cultural heritage, closely tied to the community and the natural landscape of the region.
== Religious practices == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] Historically, Koganeyama has been a central figure in the religious life of people along the Oshika Peninsula, particularly among fishermen who revered it as a guardian deity for safety and prosperity at sea. Sailors used the mountain as a navigational guide, naming different points of its visibility at sea to estimate their distance from the coast. Rituals such as lighting lamps at sunset and offering prayers and rice into the sea were common, underscoring the mountain's deep spiritual significance.
Ascetic practices were also prevalent at Mount Kinka, where ascetics engaged in rigorous spiritual exercises. Locations like the "Diamond Realm" and "Womb Realm" on the island suggest a strong tradition of esoteric Buddhism, with rituals like the "Utero Diving" symbolizing death and rebirth. This spiritual tradition, centered around the temple at Mount Kinka, attracted pilgrims and fostered a community that believed deeply in the sacred powers of the mountain and its deities, particularly Benzaiten. Over time, these practices evolved, blending with local legends and the mythology of Benzaiten as a deity of water and wealth, further enriching the cultural tapestry of the region.
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}

It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] . == Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == Koganeyama Shrine was established in the second year of the Tenpyo Shoho era (750 AD) near the site of Japan's first gold mine on Mount Kinka, vital for funding national projects like the gilding of the Todaiji Temple's Great Buddha. Initially, the shrine was dedicated to the gods of gold mining, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, and later became associated with Benzaiten, embodying prosperity and good fortune.
Legend ties the shrine to celestial origins, suggesting Benzaiten was a celestial maiden who inspired the shrine's location. Over centuries, the shrine's influence grew, supported by the Fujiwara clan among others, and became a center for Shugendo practitioners, linking spiritual practices with the region's rich gold deposits.
Despite various reconstructions due to fire and war, the shrine's cultural and spiritual significance persisted. Following the Meiji Restoration, it transitioned from a Buddhist temple to a Shinto shrine, reflecting broader religious reforms of the period. The shrine buildings, repeatedly damaged and rebuilt, today continue to serve as a site of pilgrimage and cultural heritage, closely tied to the community and the natural landscape of the region.
== Religious practices == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] {{Quote box|Relics Part 1: '''Soji Pass''' [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] Soji Pass is located in the eastern mountains of Mount Kinka. It was a sacred place inaccessible to laypeople, where the founding monk (Narizo-bo Chojun) performed the "Thousand-Day Circumambulation." At its base, there exists an ideology of a utopia deep within the mountains, akin to a hidden village view, suggesting a kind of secluded paradise. However, this might have been further localized and minimized into a "quintessentially early-modern production" after the image of Mount Kinka as a golden and silver island was formed during the Edo period. <ref name="宮田"/>。|width=30%}} Historically, Koganeyama has been a central figure in the religious life of people along the Oshika Peninsula, particularly among fishermen who revered it as a guardian deity for safety and prosperity at sea. Sailors used the mountain as a navigational guide, naming different points of its visibility at sea to estimate their distance from the coast. Rituals such as lighting lamps at sunset and offering prayers and rice into the sea were common, underscoring the mountain's deep spiritual significance.
Ascetic practices were also prevalent at Mount Kinka, where ascetics engaged in rigorous spiritual exercises. Locations like the "Diamond Realm" and "Womb Realm" on the island suggest a strong tradition of esoteric Buddhism, with rituals like the "Utero Diving" symbolizing death and rebirth. This spiritual tradition, centered around the temple at Mount Kinka, attracted pilgrims and fostered a community that believed deeply in the sacred powers of the mountain and its deities, particularly Benzaiten. Over time, these practices evolved, blending with local legends and the mythology of Benzaiten as a deity of water and wealth, further enriching the cultural tapestry of the region.
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== Pilgrims from Sendai Domain and beyond have traveled to Koganeyama Shrine for centuries, following established routes documented in travel guides like "Various Directions and Routes." The journey from Sendai to Ishinomaki splits into land and sea paths at Ishinomaki, leading to Ayukawa and then to Mount Kinka via the Omotehama and Urahama Roads. Traditional practices require land travel as a test of faith, although sea routes are also used. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims change into new straw sandals to purify themselves before visiting Daikin Temple. Strict traditions prevent removing any natural elements from the island, reflecting its sacred status. Additionally, local groups known as Koganeyama ko conduct regular worship and community gatherings, reinforcing the shrine's cultural importance. Legends and songs imbue the island with mythical qualities, celebrating its historical association with gold and prosperity. {{clear}}
== Rituals == The annual festival is held on September 25th, but there are also other Shinto rituals and festivals such as the following:
; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to purify the shrine . This is also a type of Hamadori ritual, and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
==Shrine Architecture and Features== The main hall of the shrine is designed in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall features a gabled roof with five bays across and a three-bay veranda, also with a gabled roof at the front. Both structures are topped with copper roofs. Additional buildings include a prayer hall, where goma wood is burned for prayers in a manner reminiscent of the Shugendo period, and a Suishinmon gate.
The shrine complex was gradually reconstructed over thirty years following a devastating fire in 1897. The architecture prior to this event was highly ornate, comparable in beauty to the renowned Nikko shrines, earning it the nickname "Nikko of the Eastern Frontier." Adjacent to the main hall is the site of the historic Daikin-ji Temple.
Adding to the shrine's historical allure are two bronze lanterns donated by worshippers from Yamagata Prefecture in the late 19th century. Standing 4.8 meters tall, these lanterns are celebrated as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," sharing this distinction with those at Kotohira Shrine and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple.
== Temple grounds == Mount Kinka and its entire island have long been revered as sacred, with numerous shrines and deities scattered across its landscape, including Ryuzo Gongen at the summit and Benzaiten, the deity of water and wealth, as central figures. The island houses various other deities in shrines like Watatsumi Shrine, Kanagui Shrine, and Hama Shrine, each associated with specific cultural and natural aspects of the region.
Designated a quasi-national park in 1979 and incorporated into Sanriku Fukko National Park in 2015, the area protects its rich religious and natural heritage. Key annual festivals are held in these shrines, continuing traditions that date back centuries. The temple grounds are also a site for unique 'mountain climbing' tours, which explore both the spiritual and physical elements of the landscape.
Protected as messengers of the gods, approximately 530 wild deer live on the island, reflecting the deep spiritual connection between the local wildlife and the shrine's practices. Historical and modern legends surrounding these deer emphasize their sacred status and the area's ongoing cultural significance.

; Hatsumi Festival : This ritual is held for seven days from the first day of May, and is a successor to the faith in Benzaiten, as her messenger is a snake (mi). The main festival is held at the main shrine at the hour of the snake (10:00 [[12-hour clock|a.m.]] ) on the first day (the day of the snake), and on every Sunday during the festival, [[Shinko-shiki|a portable shrine is carried]] to the temporary shrine at Kinkazan Port. During the portable shrine procession, a ritual to purify the sea is performed in which seawater is drawn and used to purify the shrine . This is also a type of Hamadori ritual, and it is said that in the past, the portable [[Mikoshi|shrine]] was carried by young men and rushed down the mountain, into the sea, and crossed all the way to Kamejima (now Kameishi) <ref name="宮田" /> <ref name="小野寺" /> . In addition, the Snake Year Enthralling Festival is held once every 12 years in the year of the snake. ; Deer antler cutting festival : This event takes place on the first and second Sunday of October, which is the mating season for deer ( [[Sika deer]] ), and involves cutting off the antlers of male deer around the temple grounds to prevent them from harming worshippers. It is said to have started in [[1963]], and was initially performed by shrine staff, but from around the end of the Showa era or the beginning of [[Heisei period|the Heisei]] era (the end of the 20th century), groups of seko (beaters ) from Ishinomaki would capture the animals and have the priests cut them off. The captured stag is given a sacred offering of sake, after which its antlers are cut off. The antlers are then donated to the shrine and distributed to those who wish to have them. <ref>[http://www.tohoku-epco.co.jp/shiro/08_10/05doubutu/doubutu02.html 東北電力「金華山信仰と神鹿」]（平成23年7月5日閲覧）。</ref>
==Shrine Architecture and Features== The main hall of the shrine is designed in the Sanbayashi-Nagare style, while the worship hall features a gabled roof with five bays across and a three-bay veranda, also with a gabled roof at the front. Both structures are topped with copper roofs. Additional buildings include a prayer hall, where goma wood is burned for prayers in a manner reminiscent of the Shugendo period, and a Suishinmon gate.
The shrine complex was gradually reconstructed over thirty years following a devastating fire in 1897. The architecture prior to this event was highly ornate, comparable in beauty to the renowned Nikko shrines, earning it the nickname "Nikko of the Eastern Frontier." Adjacent to the main hall is the site of the historic Daikin-ji Temple.
Adding to the shrine's historical allure are two bronze lanterns donated by worshippers from Yamagata Prefecture in the late 19th century. Standing 4.8 meters tall, these lanterns are celebrated as one of the "Three Great Lanterns of Japan," sharing this distinction with those at Kotohira Shrine and Yamadera Risshakuji Temple.
== Temple grounds == Mount Kinka and its entire island have long been revered as sacred, with numerous shrines and deities scattered across its landscape, including Ryuzo Gongen at the summit and Benzaiten, the deity of water and wealth, as central figures. The island houses various other deities in shrines like Watatsumi Shrine, Kanagui Shrine, and Hama Shrine, each associated with specific cultural and natural aspects of the region.
Designated a quasi-national park in 1979 and incorporated into Sanriku Fukko National Park in 2015, the area protects its rich religious and natural heritage. Key annual festivals are held in these shrines, continuing traditions that date back centuries. The temple grounds are also a site for unique 'mountain climbing' tours, which explore both the spiritual and physical elements of the landscape.
Protected as messengers of the gods, approximately 530 wild deer live on the island, reflecting the deep spiritual connection between the local wildlife and the shrine's practices. Historical and modern legends surrounding these deer emphasize their sacred status and the area's ongoing cultural significance.

<ref name="小野寺" /><ref name="小野寺">小野寺正人「金華山信仰の展開」（『東北霊山と修験道』所収）。</ref>
'''Koganeyama Shrine''' (黄金山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.<ref>{{Cite web|title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー|url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/|access-date=2023-04-02|website=jinja-gosyuin.com}}</ref>
{{infobox shinto shrine|religious_affiliation=[[Shinto]]|image=Koganeyama-jinja Haiden.jpg|map_type=Japan|coordinates={{coordinates|38|17|52.9|N|141|33|21.6|E}}|location=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|locale=5 Kanagasaki, Ayukawahama, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture|deity=- Kanayamahiko-no-Kami - Kanayamahime-no-Kami - Heavenly Myriad Deities - Earthly Myriad Deities|festivals=September 25|festival=September 25|consecration_year=Year 750 (during the Tenpyo-shoho era)|type=Listed Minor Shrine, Former Prefectural Shrine, [[Beppyo Shrine]]|architecture_type=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing|architecture_style=Three-bay Shrine Architecture with Copper Roofing}}
It is located on Mount Kinka, an isolated island in [[Pacific Ocean|the Pacific Ocean]] opposite the southeastern tip of the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}} in [[Ishinomaki]] [[Miyagi Prefecture|City]], {{ill|10=ja|11=金華山_(宮城県)|Miyagi}} Prefecture. Its [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|former status]] was that of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], but after the war [[Beppyo shrine|it became a special listed shrine]] under [[Association of Shinto Shrines|the Association of Shinto Shrines]] .
It is located facing west on the middle of the western slope of Mt. Kinka, but since the entire island of Mt. Kinka is considered a sacred area, the shrine and Mt. Kinka (island) are sometimes used almost synonymously, and it is also commonly known as '''Koganeyama Shrine''' or '''Koganeyama Koganeyama Shrine''' . The temple is bustling with worshippers and tourists praying for worldly benefits such as prosperity in business and better luck, but before modern times it was a {{ill|10=ja|11=真言宗|Shingon Buddhism|lt=Shingon sect|en}} {{ill|10=ja|11=寺院|temple}} called '''Koganeyama Daikin-ji''', which had {{ill|10=ja|11=女人禁制|lt=no women allowed|2=en|Nyonin Kinsei}} and dedicated to [[Benzaiten]] (Benten). It is counted as one of the " '''Five Benten Shrines''' " in [[Japan]] along with [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in [[Hiroshima Prefecture]] <ref>他の五弁天は[[近江国|江州]]竹生島（[[都久夫須麻神社]]）、[[相模国|相州]]江ノ島（[[江島神社]]）、[[大和国|和州]]天川（[[天河大弁財天社]]）であった（『[[和漢三才図会]]』巻第79）。</ref>, and is counted as one of the " '''Three Holy Sites of [[Tōhoku region|Tōhoku]],''' " alongside the [[Three Mountains of Dewa]] (Dewa Sanzan) in [[Yamagata Prefecture]] and {{ill|10=ja|11=恐山|Mount Osore|lt=Osorezan|en}} in [[Aomori Prefecture]] . == Deity == Before [[Meiji period|the Meiji]] period, Benzaiten was enshrined, and in the early modern period her divine virtues of bestowing good fortune were widely publicized, and she became renowned for her remarkable divine powers in bringing worldly benefits such as good luck and prosperity, especially in bringing about financial and wealthy fortune. Her worship has continued even after she was redesignated as the current enshrined deity in the Meiji period.
== History == Koganeyama Shrine was established in the second year of the Tenpyo Shoho era (750 AD) near the site of Japan's first gold mine on Mount Kinka, vital for funding national projects like the gilding of the Todaiji Temple's Great Buddha. Initially, the shrine was dedicated to the gods of gold mining, Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, and later became associated with Benzaiten, embodying prosperity and good fortune.
Legend ties the shrine to celestial origins, suggesting Benzaiten was a celestial maiden who inspired the shrine's location. Over centuries, the shrine's influence grew, supported by the Fujiwara clan among others, and became a center for Shugendo practitioners, linking spiritual practices with the region's rich gold deposits.
Despite various reconstructions due to fire and war, the shrine's cultural and spiritual significance persisted. Following the Meiji Restoration, it transitioned from a Buddhist temple to a Shinto shrine, reflecting broader religious reforms of the period. The shrine buildings, repeatedly damaged and rebuilt, today continue to serve as a site of pilgrimage and cultural heritage, closely tied to the community and the natural landscape of the region.
== Religious practices == [[File:Kinkazan.jpg|right|thumb|180x180px| Koganeyama as seen from the {{ill|10=ja|11=牡鹿半島|Oshika Peninsula|fr|Péninsule d'Oshika|en}}]] {{Quote box|Relics Part 1: '''Soji Pass''' [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] Soji Pass is located in the eastern mountains of Mount Kinka. It was a sacred place inaccessible to laypeople, where the founding monk (Narizo-bo Chojun) performed the "Thousand-Day Circumambulation." At its base, there exists an ideology of a utopia deep within the mountains, akin to a hidden village view, suggesting a kind of secluded paradise. However, this might have been further localized and minimized into a "quintessentially early-modern production" after the image of Mount Kinka as a golden and silver island was formed during the Edo period. <ref name="宮田"/>。|width=30%}} Historically, Koganeyama has been a central figure in the religious life of people along the Oshika Peninsula, particularly among fishermen who revered it as a guardian deity for safety and prosperity at sea. Sailors used the mountain as a navigational guide, naming different points of its visibility at sea to estimate their distance from the coast. Rituals such as lighting lamps at sunset and offering prayers and rice into the sea were common, underscoring the mountain's deep spiritual significance.
Ascetic practices were also prevalent at Mount Kinka, where ascetics engaged in rigorous spiritual exercises. Locations like the "Diamond Realm" and "Womb Realm" on the island suggest a strong tradition of esoteric Buddhism, with rituals like the "Utero Diving" symbolizing death and rebirth. This spiritual tradition, centered around the temple at Mount Kinka, attracted pilgrims and fostered a community that believed deeply in the sacred powers of the mountain and its deities, particularly Benzaiten. Over time, these practices evolved, blending with local legends and the mythology of Benzaiten as a deity of water and wealth, further enriching the cultural tapestry of the region.
=== Koganeyama faith === The belief in Mount Kinka since the early modern period has focused on seeking worldly benefits such as financial luck from Benzaiten, but at its root is the expectation of the people that there is a place somewhere in the area filled with gold that will one day appear, as they long for the blessings that come from gold production. It is thought that ascetic monks took advantage of this expectation and linked Mount Kinka to the historical fact of gold production in the Tenpyo period, spreading the idea of Mount Kinka as a place where the ideals of the people had become reality, thus expanding the sphere of belief. Eventually, people around Mount Kinka came to believe that gold was buried in a corner of the island, or that Mount Kinka was an island made of gold, even though the island is almost entirely made of [[granite]] and has no gold veins. [[:ja:西川如見|Nishikawa Nyoken]] wrote, "If you look at the map of the world and see that there is an island of gold and silver in the East Sea of Japan, it would not be this island (Mount Kinka) <ref name="西川">西川如見『長崎夜話草』、[[享保]]4年（1719年）。</ref> " He accepted [[Europe|the European notion]] of Japan as an island of gold and silver, as represented by [[Marco Polo]] 's The Travels of Marco Polo, and applied this notion to Mount Kinka in a more localized way. <ref>なお、[[天明]]8年（1788年）当時の伝聞として、金華山に「黄金満ち満ち、参詣の山道砂金あり」という風評があるが「甚だしき虚説にして、山中においてはさらに金色の石なし」という報告がある（古川前掲書）。</ref>{{Quote box|Relics Part 2: '''Golden Sea Cucumber''' (Kinko) [[file:Gthumb.svg|left]] The sea cucumbers that grow near Mount Kinka are called "Golden Sea Cucumbers (Kinko)," named for consuming the gold sands found on Mount Kinka. According to Sakuma Dongon, they are deep yellow in color, similar to chicken eggs, which he describes as a manifestation of "gold energy"<ref name="橘">橘前掲書巻之五。</ref>. This connection to the gold-producing legends is significant. Dongon notes that they are characterized by their round shape with a distinctive scar on the back. According to Tachibana Nanki, they are smaller compared to other sea cucumbers, have a unique taste, and the dried and hardened ones are highly prized throughout Japan<ref name="橘"/>, and Furukawa Komatsuan also notes that they have a golden color on their back, distinctly different from other sea cucumbers<ref name="古川">古川古松軒『東遊雑記』巻之十。</ref>. |width=35%}}
==== '''Pilgrimage to Koganeyama and Koganeyama Ko''' ==== Pilgrims from Sendai Domain and beyond have traveled to Koganeyama Shrine for centuries, following established routes documented in travel guides like "Various Directions and Routes." The journey from Sendai to Ishinomaki splits into land and sea paths at Ishinomaki, leading to Ayukawa and then to Mount Kinka via the Omotehama and Urahama Roads. Traditional practices require land travel as a test of faith, although sea routes are also used. Upon reaching Mount Kinka, pilgrims change into new straw sandals to purify themselves before visiting Daikin Temple. Strict traditions prevent removing any natural elements from the island, reflecting its sacred status. Additionally, local groups known as Koganeyama ko conduct regular worship and community gatherings, reinforcing the shrine's cultural importance. Legends and songs imbue the island with mythical qualities, celebrating its historical association with gold and prosperity. {{clear}}
